line: No white lighters ’til I fuck my twenty-eighth up (Fire)
vault_lines: No white lighters 'til I fuck my twenty-eighth up (Fire)
meaning:
Several famous musicians associated with the 27 Club, most notably Jimi Hendrix, Janis Joplin, Jim Morrison, Amy Winehouse, and Kurt Cobain, became linked to a pattern claiming that they died with white lighters in their possession, creating a superstition that carrying or using white lighters brings bad luck, more ominously for musicians evoking the fate of artists who haven’t made it past 27.



Jim Morrison, Amy Winehouse, and Kurt Cobain

Frank plays into this superstition by refusing to use a white lighter until he can “fuck [his] twenty-eighth up”. Once he makes it through 27, he can light up without worrying about the same fate, making the escape from death feel like a celebration rather than just turning 28.



The number 28 also appears in Frank’s own life through his birthday. He was born on October 28, 1987, making his 28th his golden birthday, the day you turn the same age as the day of the month you were born.

Another layer to this line is the weed reference. An ounce is approximately 28.35 grams, meaning one gram is roughly one twenty-eighth of an ounce, turning “twenty-eighth” into another meaning inside a line about using a lighter. Frank had previously touched on this on Odd Future’s “Oldie”:

Drive around with your friends, smoke a gram of that haze
Bro, easy on the ounce, that’s a lot for a day

Collapsing several meanings into the same number: 27 is the age of the curse, 28 represents surviving it, October 28 is Frank’s birthday, and roughly 1/28 of an ounce is a gram of weed, all converging on “twenty-eighth.”

Nirvana is a phenomenon that exists in Buddhist traditions, although other religions have similar concepts that can be loosely tied to nirvana. It can be thought of as reaching a state of total enlightenment or self-realization. Some believe that people enter a state of final nirvana when they die.

Similarly, Frank Ocean wants to experience this eternal euphoria, but he chooses to do so through drugs instead of death.

Additionally, this could also be some clever wordplay giving a slight nod to Kurt Cobain, the frontman of the grunge band Nirvana—Ocean wants to “see Nirvana” but doesn’t want to die to do so, seeing as Cobain is dead.

Frank Ocean is reminiscing about his youth in New Orleans, when he saw the frequent activities of No Limit Records founder Percy “Master P” Miller and former label VP and P’s long-time business partner Anthony “Boz” Boswell.

Morton, were building massive mansions for themselves by preaching to others about obtaining wealth; all the lead pastors within Morton’s Full Gospel Baptist Church Fellowship use the title of “bishop.” However, their prosperity doctrine did not resonate with Ocean as his family struggled in poverty; back when trips to the fairly inexpensive restaurant Shoney’s were reserved only for special occasions.

line: After ’Trina hit, I had to transfer campus (Yeah, yeah)
vault_lines: After 'Trina hit, I had to transfer campus (Yeah, yeah)
meaning:
One week after starting his first year at the University of New Orleans in August 2005, Hurricane Katrina hit Frank Ocean’s hometown and forced him to transfer campuses to the University of Louisiana at Lafayette, where he studied for one semester before dropping out.

Katrina was a category 5 tropical cyclone and the costliest storm in U.S. history, causing an estimated $125 billion in damages—more than half of which occurred in New Orleans. With his hometown in pieces, Ocean decided to move to Los Angeles, later telling the BBC in 2012:

[Katrina] itself didn’t make me move, but the storm ruined my recording environment and the studio I was working in got looted and destroyed by floodwater. I didn’t have a place to work in New Orleans, so I left and came to LA.

Ocean arrived in the City of Angels in 2006 and eventually found a foothold in the music industry by writing songs for other people. In 2010, he joined Odd Future and started making a name for himself.

If Katrina had fizzled out in the Atlantic, who knows how things might have turned out for Mr. Ocean.

Frank Ocean has credited his grandfather, Lionel McGruder, as the only father-figure he’s ever known, but he has since passed on. Ocean dedicated his 2016 magazine Boy Don’t Cry to Lionel, his aunt Janet, and his childhood friend Matthew Lacey.

Growing up, Lionel gave Ocean the nickname “Lonny,” which his friends & family still call him today. After Lionel’s passing in 2010, Ocean dedicated the track “There Will Be Tears” on his 2011 mixtape nostalgia, ULTRA to his late grandfather. Ocean also drew inspiration from Lionel for the song “Crack Rock” on his 2012 debut studio album channel ORANGE; Lionel served as a mentor to fellow recovering addicts at Alcoholics Anonymous & Narcotics Anonymous meetings, which made an impression on Ocean, telling The Guardian in 2012:

My grandfather was a mentor for NA and AA groups. I used to go to the meetings and hear the addicts: heroin and crack and alcohol. Stories like that influence a song like “Crack Rock.”

“Cleve” is most likely Cleve Jones, an activist for LGBT and AIDS rights whose San Francisco AIDS Foundation is one of the biggest support organizations in the U.S. Malik Shakur, Tupac’s nephew, tweeted a photo of Cleve Jones captioned with this lyric on the day “Lens” dropped.

Matthew Lacey is a photographer and Ocean’s childhood best friend. Matthew inspired the eponymous character in Ocean’s six-part screenplay “Godspeed,” published in Boys Don’t Cry, which Ocean described in the magazine’s opening letter as “basically a reimagined part of my boyhood.” The protagonist of the text is Steely, a character loosely based on Ocean himself; in the play’s introduction, the character Matthew is described as “Steely’s childhood friend akin to a brother.” Matthew also received a shoutout from Ocean in “Futura Free,” the closing track of Ocean’s second studio album Blonde, released in companion with the Boys Don’t Cry in 2016.

I was still in my car telling myself it was gonna be fine and to take deep breaths. I took the breaths and carried on. This complicated relationship blossomed from a long-time friendship, and here the friend tells him that they intimately love him, when Frank all this time thought he could never love him back and had likely begun to accept that fact. Elvis Presley is an American rock and roll singer who passed away in 1977. He is known as the “King of Rock and Roll” and is often credited with changing the entirety of pop culture in America at the peak of his fame in the 1960s and 70s.

While still performing and creating music, Elvis was highly influenced by African-American artists of his era, but was able to share his music with a larger audience due to the African-American artists not having an equivalent platform to white artists. Presley was open about his influences and relative musical skill to these African-American artists, as seen in the following quote:

A lot of people seem to think I started this business. But rock ‘n’ roll was here a long time before I came along. Nobody can sing that kind of music like coloured people. Let’s face it: I can’t sing like Fats Domino can. I know that.

In the same way that rock ‘n’ roll was appropriated from African-American artists and made into “pop” for white audiences, we now see hip-hop and RnB, genres traditionally filled with African-American creators, being exposed to larger, white audiences by new white hip-hop and RnB artists such as Eminem, Machine Gun Kelly, and G-Eazy. The genre that they operate in is not new nor did they do anything to create it, but they were able to expose a larger audience to it simply because of the color of their skin.

Frank also may be referring to how his musical style has also been regarded in a revolutionary manner, with many critics viewing his music as revolutionary within its own hip-hop and R&B genres. Frank, however, seems to comment on his peers around his who think that they are revolutionary artists, disapproving of their opinions of themselves.

In 2006, Frank Ocean relocated to Los Angeles, California, to pursue a career in the music industry. In a 2012 interview with GQ, Ocean spoke about the move:

I had been putting together these demos that I was going to properly record in a real studio in LA. So I saved up money doing Sheetrocking, and I drove out with my girlfriend at the time. I was only supposed to be there for six weeks. I don’t feel like I ever made a conscious decision to stay six years. You just kind of roll. The first four-and-a-half years was me in the studio every day, writing songs for other people.

However, before the release of his 2016 visual album Endless and studio album Blonde, Ocean kept himself hidden from the public eye and moved around silently, recording his two projects. Although he could have kept himself in the limelight of fame in the big city, as he did early on in his career, Ocean decided to move away from the chaos and live a “quieter” life on the outside.

line: And if acts of God breaks us apart Least we did ours
vault_lines: And if acts of God breaks us apart
meaning:
This phrase could be interpreted as a surrender to fate – by invoking the will of God, Frank is appealing to the belief that all actions are preordained and out of human control.

If God destined things to be this way, muses Frank, at least we did us perfect. This is necessarily true – if God preordains everything, there was no way that Frank and his partner could do anything but be perfect. This is therefore a tacit acceptance of their troubled relationship – it is what it is, and it can’t be anything else.

It’s important to note that this isn’t necessarily an admission of religious faith from Frank – he appeals to a popular image that shapes fate, but determinism can exist without a supreme figure.

line: It’s all new to me It’s all new to me Having you around It’s all new to me It’s all new to me Having you ’round the Higgs
vault_lines: It's all new to me
meaning:
Frank describes their relationship as intimate as mother-son relation but he knows that eventually it will come to an end. The “son” will leave him.

Interestingly, though the love in the preceding lines is described as “mothers,” it’s here illustrated as a mother-son relationship. As the love itself is motherly, one can assume that Frank is further stretching the metaphor to make himself the mother.

This doesn’t necessarily reflect their positions in the relationship. Frank paints himself as the “mother” to stress that it is his partner who is leaving him, much like a son leaves home and becomes independent.

The meaning of “Higgs,” after which the track is named, is mysterious – though The Higgs are a four-piece band in LA, most affiliate the term with the Higgs-Boson, a scientific concept pertaining to particle physics theory.

line: All this time I knew That average was something to fall back on after genius ends

meaning:
In this line, genius shouldn’t be taken so literally. Instead of referring to Ocean’s musical prowess, it likely means that the dullness that comprises most of our lives is what inevitably follows the rare moments of human ecstasy.

“Genius” therefore represents the peak of his happiness, whilst “average” represents normal, everyday emotions.

Most of Frank’s songs are self-contained short stories, and since the song is about a failed relationship, this interpretation fits really well – all good things come to an end, and falling back on average is the way in which they do so.

line: Keeping us warm Walking in straight lines
vault_lines: Walking in straight lines
meaning:
Straight from the get go, Frank serves up a helping of social commentary. Ocean’s lyric recalls the Tears For Fears song “Mad World”:

Bright and early for their daily races
Going nowhere, going nowhere

It’s also remarkably similar to Echosmith’s pop sleeper “Cool Kids”:

She seems them walking in a straight line
That’s not really her style

All three sets of lyrics hark back to one idea: the binds of society on the common citizen to follow a certain manner of life. The way modern society is organized is that people are essentially locked into a specific routine, the equivalent of the metaphorical “straight line.” Ocean remarks how culture boxes us into a limited amount of choices in life due to overwhelming rules and regulations, which is ironic given the common perception that we’re living in a free society.

line: Ménage on my birthday, tap out on the first stroke
vault_lines: Ménage on my birthday, tap out on the first stroke
meaning:
A ménage is a French term that essentially means a household for three. It is an arrangement where a married couple and a lover of one of them live together while sharing sexual relations.

In this line, Frank twists the idea to emphasize imbalance and resentment toward the male partner. Instead of the typical setup of one man and two women, the lyric suggests a triangle between Frank, a woman, and her boyfriend.

Earlier lines imply Frank has taken the man’s girlfriend, leaving the boyfriend present but sidelined. In this context, the man is reduced to a passive role, metaphorically placed in a ‘cuckchair’ within the ménage, watching rather than participating. This use of “ménage” underscores power, displacement, and quiet humiliation rather than mutual desire.

meaning:
The theremin is an electronic instrument played by the movement of a person’s hands in the air, which allows them to control both its volume & frequency. The theremin is known for its eerie, somewhat off-putting sound and was often reserved to science fiction films before being popularized by The Beach Boys after the instrument was used in their acclaimed song “Good Vibrations.” This likely was no coincidence, as Ocean stated in a 2013 NME interview:

When I was making the first [album], there were a group of artists that I listened to just for inspiration and to absorb the energies. It was a lot of Stevie Wonder, and this time, it’s a lot of Beach Boys and Beatles and whatnot. So we’ll see how it trickles into the music and the final product. I can’t say much other than that.

The Beatles are credited in the tracks “White Ferrari” & “Seigfried” for the use of their melodies and samples. The theremin is used several tracks prior during the instrumental interlude of “Skyline To.”

Though the popularity of castrati voices began to decline in the 1700s, the practice of creating castrati was not banned in Italy until 1870.

line: Beans, Starbucks, starstruck
vault_lines: Love that I, love that I give
meaning:
On December 18, 2018, Frank Ocean posted a video to his Instagram story featuring a snippet of an unreleased track, later know as “DHL.” The audio excerpt began in the middle of this line—Beans, Starbucks, starstruck—notably, beginning after the word “beans.”

Later, on February 5, 2019, a series of cryptic posts appeared on Ocean’s Tumblr; a hacker identifying himself as SpirDark claimed to possess unreleased music by Ocean with notable guest features:


Post #1: ? (2019) ? (2019) ? (2020).

Post #2: MARCH 1ST / SOLANA [SZA] + KL [Kendrick Lamar] + ANDRE [André 3000] / HERE FOR THE BEANS.

Post #3: IF YOU DIDN’T LIKE 2018, YOU WILL DEFINITELY LIKE 2019.

Post #6: “SPIRDARK.” 2019 COMEBACK (SOON). NOBODY IS SAFE. EMAIL ME IF YOU’RE INTERESTED IN BUYING UNRELEASED FRANK SONGS / [Redacted: SpirDark’s email address].

Post #7: If this post gets 25,000 likes, I will release the Frank Ocean song featuring Andre, Kendrick, and SZA (it’s a legit song) / [Redacted: link to an Instagram post by an unrelated person; trolling].


It would later be reported that Ocean’s team quietly contacted the New York Attorney General’s Office in early 2019, after one of his producers discovered a remote user had gained unauthorized access to his Dropbox files.

Ocean’s hacked Tumblr posts quickly circulated online, with many fans questioning their meaning or veracity. This speculation would intensify after sleuths on Reddit noticed that Ocean had followed an Instagram account a day before the hack with the username: @here.for.the.beans. After receiving many new followers, the Instagram user would seemingly confirm their connection to the Tumblr hack with a nonsensical post referencing Ocean, which they later deleted. After various news outlets reported on the unusual Tumblr posts and Instagram account, Ocean unfollowed @here.for.the.beans. The intentions behind the account, or why Ocean initially followed them, remain unclear—the Instagram profile may have served as a means of communication between SpirDark & Ocean or another unspecified purpose or exploit.

Although nothing can be said for certain, the Tumblr post and Instagram handle, “here for the beans,” may reference this line in “DHL”—Beans, Starbucks, starstruck. The phrase might have been SpirDark’s way of taunting Ocean by alluding to material in his unreleased tracks, particularly by using part of a line that Ocean had recently teased to the public. To a lesser degree, “here for the beans” could also be interpreted as SpirDark being “here for the money,” an expression similar to that of “bringing home the bacon” or “making dough.” Alternatively, “the beans” could reference some unreleased content that remains unheard by the public, possibly a track featuring Kendrick Lamar, SZA, and André 3000, as alluded to in the Tumblr posts.

The true meaning behind the madness—if one can be determined—will likely never be known, absent clarification by SpirDark or Ocean.

On September 12, 2019, UK authorities arrested SpirDark (A. Kwiatkowski, age 20) in Ipswich, England, finding 1,263 unreleased songs by 89 different artists on his hard drives. According to City of London Police, his exploits netted him £131,000 in cryptocurrency sales of unreleased music. On October 21, 2022, a judge sentenced SpirDark to 18 months in prison for criminal offenses related to his hacking activities, and on May 26, 2023, the Ipswich Crown Court granted a confiscation order of his assets worth approximately £101,500 (£51,975 + 2.64 Bitcoin).

You know, it’s funny talking about it these days because I couldn’t really tell anybody anything for a couple of years. Couldn’t tell anyone at the label, obviously. But I also couldn’t talk with anyone at Apple because the industry is too small and it would’ve gotten back to the label for sure.

Frank planned on staying for just 6 weeks, but he never went back.

I couldn’t really tell anybody anything for a couple of years. Couldn’t tell anyone at the label, obviously. But I also couldn’t talk with anyone at Apple because the industry is too small and it would’ve gotten back to the label for sure. So I kept it to myself and a few in my circle. Frank’s connection with his hard drives was first revealed in his interview with New York Times on November 15, 2016, and was talked about in his W Magazine feature on September 30, 2019.

He continues to say “stealin' and robbin'” alongside with the former to explain how “crackheads” will do anything for the next hit once addicted. Note: One notable case of a crooked cop was Barry Seal, a former CIA operative who worked with various cartels to ship cocaine on to a field in Mena, Arkansas. This fits in with why Frank chose to mention Arkansas in the first verse of the song.

Fun Fact: In an interview with Oyster Magazine Frank mentioned he sold crack in high school:


ZB: What were you like in school?

FO: I was a thug. I sold a lot of cocaine and crack.

“The gutter” is a commonly used metaphor; living in the gutter representing the lowest point of human existence and experience. In this case it’s the aftermath of addiction.

Frank also points out the fact that if a black man is shot, he gets a lot less media attention than if a cop – crooked or otherwise – is shot. For cops, they send out hundreds looking for the shooter, but there is no justice for the shooting of an average civilian.

It’s hypocrisy considering the terrible influence crooked cops have on the community. The cop becomes a martyr even though he is part of the problem.

Note: At the time of the song’s release, the death of Trayvon Martin was big in the news.

Ocean has publicly discussed his personal life on a few occasions. In the missive, Ocean describes falling in love with a man during the summers of his 19th & 20th years on Earth. The ‘coming out’ letter would circulate online, generating positive discussion in the days after & years since its publication, empowering others to tell their own stories.

meaning:
Frank Ocean recorded his 2016 albums Endless & Blonde at various recording studios across the world, including but not limited to:


Abbey Road Studios (London, England) – the most famous studio in the world; where The Beatles (major influence on Ocean) recorded most of their music for EMI in the 1960s; Ocean recorded parts of Endless & Blonde in Studio Three & the Penthouse, assisted by recording engineer Matt Mysko.
EastWest Studios (Hollywood, California) – Ocean recorded parts of his 2012 album channel ORANGE in Studio Two & Three; Ocean later recorded parts of Endless & Blonde in Studio Two & Five.
Electric Lady Studios (New York, New York) – founded by Jimi Hendrix in 1970; Ocean recorded parts of Endless & Blonde in Studio A, mixed by Tom Elmhirst in Studio C.
Shangri-La (Malibu, California) – a ranch property with bungalow, converted to a recording studio by Rob Fraboni to the specs of Bob Dylan in the 1970s; purchased by Rick Rubin (co-founder of Def Jam & friend of Ocean) in 2011; Ocean shared a photo of the studio alongside a list of his favorite songs in his 2016 Blonde-companion Boys Don’t Cry magazine.
Capitol Studios (Hollywood, California) – nested in the historic Capitol Records Tower, which hosted Ocean’s listening party for channel ORANGE in 2012; Ocean recorded parts of Endless & Blonde in Studios A & C.
Question de Son (Paris, France) – where Ocean recorded parts of Endless & Blonde, alongside French composer Christophe Chassol; where Ocean later recorded his 2020 singles “Cayendo” & “Dear April.”



“365 twelve-hour blocks” is equivalent to 4,380 hours or 182.5 days of rented studio time (likely hyperbole).

Frank Ocean catalogs the cost of retaining the rights to the master recordings of his 2016 album Blonde, breaking free from his contract with Def Jam after his 2016 visual album Endless.

Initially, Ocean likely intended the foldout to be a functional lyric sheet but later transformed it into a piece of art. There is a stigma towards tattoos in Japan, which has a long and convoluted history. In modern Japan, tattoos (or “irezumi”) are usually associated with either fashion or the yakuza, an organized crime group similar to the Mafia whose members often have tattoos to indicate their loyalty.

During Japan’s Edo period, tattoos were a form of punishment that would distinguish criminals within society. Tattoos were also commonly associated with Japan’s working class population. Even today, there are many forms of social exclusion in Japan for those with tattoos.



The most common place to see a sign like this is in a traditional Japanese bathhouse, continuing the heated pool theme from previous lines.



Tattoos are closely linked with a person’s identity as they are often personal and literally permanently inked onto a person’s skin. In Japan, tattoos are generally not seen as acceptable in mainstream society and culture. meaning:
Frank Ocean’s male partner’s physique contains features that reflect those of a female, although he displays a masculine side through fighting others. Ocean likens the duality of his partner to Chanel, a luxurious fashion company whose iconic logo shows two opposing C’s.

Chanel’s logo and Frank Ocean wearing a Chanel glasses case while walking around SoHo in New York City (Robert Kamau, 2017-06-21).

Duality is a recurring motif throughout Ocean’s discography, often being touched upon when discussing his bisexuality—most famously explored in “Nights.” Interestingly, as reported in Lisa Chaney’s biography Coco Chanel: An Intimate Life, the brand’s founder, Gabrielle “Coco” Chanel, was revealed to be bisexual.

It is worth noting that the line “See on both sides like Chanel” is a homophone for “C on both sides like Chanel,” as well as being a close homophone of “sea on both sides like channel.” A channel is a waterway between two bodies of land; some of which can be created by a sea and defined as an ocean channel. Because channels act as a division between landmasses, it can be speculated that the line is meant to correlate with the saying “there’s plenty of fish in the sea,” as well as establishing Ocean’s preference for swimming in pool water.

These lyrics became famous almost instantaneously. Only ten days after the song’s release, The Undefeated labeled “Chanel” as “the most important song in the world right now.” Later, on December 7, 2017, the opening line was featured on Pitchfork’s list of “The 15 Lyrics That Defined 2017.” Furthermore, Billboard ranked the song as the 26th best of 2017, putting major emphasis on the correlation between Chanel’s logo & Ocean’s sexuality. At the time, the army was under investigation by the senate for suspected Communist members during a time of consistent political repression. They targeted persons suspected of being Communists or with views deemed unsavory, and fired, arrested, or blacklisted those who they viewed as disloyal.

meaning:
Solipsism is the belief that the only thing that’s actually real is one’s own experiences and thoughts.  It comes from the Latin Solus Ipse, roughly “alone self.” From a solipsistic perspective, reality would be something like a dream that the observer is having.



Solipsism has a long history as a philosophical problem; it seems absurd to common sense, but is remarkably difficult to come up with purely logical arguments against. It’s also a psychological experience described by people with mental illness or serious neurological damage. People without any  conditions also describe solipsistic experiences, often as part of an existential crisis.

Solipsism is also colloquially used as a synonym for extreme egotism and narcissism, which may be partly Frank’s meaning here: he’s confessing to a high degree self-absorption that’s become all encompassing.

line: This guy has “Slave” on his face You think he wanted the masters with his masters?

meaning:
In 1993, Prince was involved in a highly contentious fight with his longtime record label Warner Bros. Records. He felt he didn’t have full artistic control as he and the label argued over the direction of his music. Prince was also not happy with the financial aspects of his contract, including the fact that the label owned the masters of his music, meaning the record label controlled the sounds in the master recordings and could collect royalties as they license Prince’s music to third parties—even without his permission.



His frustration with the music business inspired him to write the word “slave” on his cheek and change his name to an unpronounceable “love symbol” in protest, leading him to be referred to as “The Artist Formerly Known as Prince"—or simply just "The Artist"—and releasing his music through his own NPG Records label. In a 1996 interview with Rolling Stone, he discussed his thought process on the situation:

People think I’m a crazy fool for writing ‘slave’ on my face. But if I can’t do what I want to do, what am I? When you stop a man from dreaming, he becomes a slave. That’s where I was. I don’t own Prince’s music. If you don’t own your masters, your master owns you.

Prince went back to using his name in 2000, and after a long battle, he was able to gain control of the masters for his back catalog from Warner Bros. in 2014. Based on the other lines in this verse, Jay seems to be suggesting that Prince’s estate—his family and his attorney L. Londell McMillan—are essentially selling him out to the highest bidder. Despite the fact that Jay “sat down with Prince, eye to eye” to discuss how he wanted his music handled going forward—such as only having his music streamed through the artist-owned TIDAL service—Jay feels Prince’s estate has their own money-making agenda. line: On my lapel, at the table, I’m givin’ a toast (Givin’ it, clink) The first weddin’ that I’ve been in my twenties Thinkin’ maybe someone is not somethin’ to own Maybe the government got nothin’ to do with it
vault_lines: On my lapel, at the table, I'm givin' a toast (Givin' it, clink)
meaning:
Frank is at the beginning of the phase in his life where all the friends around him are getting married. This is not the first time Frank has made a comment on the nature of weddings. On “American Wedding” from his debut mixtape, nostaliga, ULTRA, Frank attacked the institution of marriage in the USA:

It’s just an American wedding
They don’t mean too much, they don’t last enough
We had an American wedding
Now what’s mine is yours, American divorce

Here he reflects on similar views. He sees two issues with marriage, firstly the interference of the government; he believes the state should have nothing to do with love. This could be as a result of his sexuality, since it was illegal for two men to marry in the US until June of 2015. He sings on “We All Try”:

I believe that marriage isn’t
Between a man and woman but between love and love

Although gay marriage is now legal, his sentiments against institutionalized love still remain. He talked more about this in the poem “Boyfriend” from his Boys Don’t Cry magazine:

I could say that I’m happy
They let me and my boyfriend become married
I could say that I’m happy
But cross my heart I didn’t notice

His second problem with marriage seems to be about its permanence. He believes someone shouldn’t be “owned” by another person.

There is also a reference to the contraction of “Mrs.” While now it is pronounced “misses” it was once pronounced “Mister’s”, indicating the ownership of a man.

Mafia is a key figure in many of Frank Ocean’s early songs, especially before Frank’s mainstream breakthrough. He’s known by his subtle tag — a soft female voice whispering “Mafia” — which appears in several early tracks.

The two first met during a Brandy recording session in 2008. At the time, Frank was still writing under the name Lonny Breaux , and Mafia was part of the production duo MIDI Mafia. After that meeting, they started working closely together, recording demos and writing songs that would shape the early stages of Frank’s sound.

Mafia helped Frank develop tracks like “Swim Good”, which later appeared on nostalgia, ULTRA, as well as “One Look”, “No Bonnie”, and “Miss You So” — all of which have become fan favorites, even if some remain officially unreleased. These collaborations often blended emotional lyrics with cinematic, minimalist production, foreshadowing the unique style Frank would later become known for.

In recent years, however, Frank and Mafia haven’t been seen working together. There have been no public collaborations or signs of ongoing communication. Still, Mafia’s role in Frank’s early career is significant, especially in helping him transition from a behind-the-scenes songwriter into a solo artist with his own vision.

“This Is Mom” is the title of a 2016 interview with Watson published in Boys Don’t Cry magazine, released in companion with Blonde, where she discussed her legendary voicemails:

I think when you call someone, you should leave a voicemail for them. But with my son [Jonathan], I do leave voicemails for him, I’ll often leave inspirational voicemails. Sometimes I leave nasty voicemails too! And I’ll leave nasty voicemails for Lonny [Frank Ocean] too, when the timing is right! line: [Skit: Rosie Watson]
vault_lines: Not to drink alcohol, not to use drugs
meaning:
Rosie Watson is the mother of one of Frank Ocean’s childhood friends, Jonathan Ikpeazu; known as “Auntie Rosie” to Ocean, Watson is not his mom (that’s Katonya Breaux), but she has served as a motherly figure in the lives of her son’s friends. This voicemail is similar to “Not Just Money” on Ocean’s debut album channel ORANGE, which she also performed. She is known to leave voicemail messages that give advice or inspiration, pairing well with her profession as a therapist & clinical psychologist.

In a 2016 interview with Watson titled “This Is Mom,” published in Ocean’s Boys Don’t Cry magazine (released in companion with Blonde), she was asked: Your voicemails are [the] stuff of legends; what do you love about leaving people messages?

I think when you call someone, you should leave a voicemail for them. But with my son [Jonathan], I do leave voicemails for him, I’ll often leave inspirational voicemails. Sometimes I leave nasty voicemails too! And I’ll leave nasty voicemails for Lonny [Frank Ocean] too, when the timing is right! I want them to always remember to just be themselves, they don’t have to be the type of man described in a rap song. They don’t have to be balling, they don’t have to be ballers, they don’t have to be shot callers. I leave voicemails for my son in particular because I want my son to remain optimistic. I want him to know that his mother has his back, no matter what. I want Lonny to also know that Auntie Rosie is here for him.

The interview also mentions what prompted the call; she intended to warn Frank Ocean (or her son, Jonathan) of the “flesh-eating bacteria roaming rampant on college campuses,” more than likely referring to meningococcus (Neisseria meningitidis). While not a “flesh-eating” bacteria, meningococcus can cause meningitis, inflammation of the protective membranes around the brain & spinal cord that, in severe cases, leads to the life-threatening destruction of nerve cells. College students are prone to contracting the disease because of their close proximity to each other, especially those living in campus dormitories, and the prevalence of social events which may involve the sharing of food or beverages, or kissing.

In 2005, Ocean, then “Lonny” Breaux, graduated from John Ehret High School and enrolled in the University of New Orleans, majoring in English. His studies were immediately disrupted in August 2005 by Hurricane Katrina, destroying his home & personal recording studio, leading him to transfer to the University of Louisiana at Lafayette, where he briefly attended before dropping out to focus on his music career & relocating to Los Angeles, California.

During the 2005–2006 academic year, the University of Louisiana at Lafayette experienced an outbreak of meningococcal disease; in January & February of 2006, five cases were reported to the Louisiana Office of Public Health, resulting in the deaths of two students. It’s possible Auntie Rosie heard about the outbreak on the news, and concerned for either Frank or Jonathan’s safety, made the phone call & now-famous voicemail.

It’s generally recommended, especially during an outbreak of meningococcus, to avoid sharing drinks & cigarettes to prevent the spread of disease; to that effect, “Be Yourself” is backed by the advice of medical professionals, in addition to containing otherwise solid motherly guidance for “many college students.”

line: I guess it couldn’t hurt me
vault_lines: I guess it couldn't hurt me
meaning:
Romantic love, particularly unfulfilled romantic love, has been portrayed as a kind of worship—loving and revering an untouchable figure—throughout history of the written word. This religion is wrong though, because it hurts him and brings him down, literally, to his knees. Love is well known for its ability to make people both literally and figuratively sick, and Frank is willing both to take his medicine and to convert his faith in the pursuit of personal wellness.

However, another level of these lines warns against not just love, but any religion that brings a person to their knees. This can be read as an allusion most institutionalized religions such as Christianity and Islam, where kneeling down is a common practice while at prayer.

In the wake of Orlando mass shooting which killed 49 patrons of a gay club, Frank Ocean posted an open letter questioning why some religious people believe that God wants them to hurt, even kill, others for not following what they believe to be God’s law.

Since Frank is expressing his unrequited love for a man in this song, he may be saying that if he has to beg forgiveness for loving someone, then that is a bad religion because it doesn’t accept people as they are, and instead tries to break them.

line: Oh-oh-oh, only bad, only bad religion Could have me feelin’ the way I do
vault_lines: Oh-oh-oh, only bad, only bad religion
meaning:
Frank recognizes that his feelings—the pain of being in love with someone who could never love him back—are unhealthy. He knows he needs to break free of this stagnant relationship, but even at the end of the song he’s unsure how to accomplish this.

Frank could also be calling out communities, not necessarily just religious ones, whose beliefs lead them condemn queerness, causing incredible mental anguish to the LGBTQ+ people in those communities who feel alienated and “sick” with the supposed wrongness of their feelings. As Frank explained in his tumblr post on the Orlando shootings,

Many hate us and wish we didn’t exist. Many are annoyed by our wanting to be married like everyone else or use the correct restroom like everyone else. Many don’t see anything wrong with passing down the same old values that send thousands of kids into suicidal depression each year. So we say pride and we express love for who and what we are. Because who else will in earnest?

meaning:
This is a reference to the Jonestown Massacre and Reverend Jim Jones, the man who originated the Peoples Temple in the 1950s–1970s.

On November 18, 1978, Jim Jones infamously directed the mass murder–suicide of his followers at their compound in Guyana by leading/coercing them to drink Flavor Aid poisoned with cyanide and other sedatives, before shooting himself. This event gave rise to the phrase “drinking the Kool-Aid,” or blindly accepting a foolish ideology based only upon the overpowering coaxing of another.

An unrequited love can be just as self-destructive as joining a cult—you lose sight of reality and the bigger picture because you’re obsessed over one person or idea.




 The vat used to mix the grape Favor Aid–cyanide cocktail in Jonestown, Guyana; in the background, an assortment of pill bottles, vials, syringes & paper cups (Frank Johnston, 1978).




Jones made an audio recording of the events preceding & during the massacre, known as the Jonestown "Death Tape" (FBI No. Q042).

line: I can never make him love me Never make him love me
vault_lines: I can never make him love me
meaning:
This hook is the most overt depiction of love for a man on the album. It’s likely inspired by the man from Frank’s open letter about his first love, who didn’t return his feelings.

Frank posted this letter one week before he debuted “Bad Religion” on Jimmy Fallon in July of 2012. The resultant media fervor about his emotional “coming out” helped to propel Frank and the song into the mainstream consciousness.

Listeners may also hear the “him” of the song as “Him”, prompting them to interpret the song in another way: Frank can’t make a God that frowns upon homosexuality love him.

line: Ooh, ooh, this unrequited love To me, it’s nothin’ but a one-man cult
vault_lines: Ooh, ooh, this unrequited love
meaning:
Un-returned affection can often build to fanatical devotion, especially if you internalize it as Frank Ocean did. Cults are often formed around a charismatic leader who uses his followers to advance his own agenda without truly devoting himself to them. Their followers are often conditioned to believe that there is no way to live outside of the strictures set by the cult leader. People often say love is blind, but these lines go one step further and imply that unrequited love is like being brainwashed.

Jim Jones with a member of the Peoples Temple

Here, Ocean is the only person forming this cult around the object of his affections, leaving him lonely both from unrequited love and from not having other worshippers who understand his devotion.

Ocean’s unrequited love could be for a deity or a romantic interest. While the imagery & title of the song suggest a theological, spiritual love interest, the idea of a one-man cult could represent Ocean feeling entrapped in fondness for a more physical individual who won’t love him back.

meaning:
The “bad religion” is his “unrequited love”— the entire song functions as an exorcism of Frank Ocean’s grief, bitterness, and disappointment at the failure of his first love.

He’s basically saying that he worshiped his first lover in a way that is similar to how one might worship God. That’s also why he uses the phrase “one-man cult.” Cults have an excessive, often dangerous admiration for a particular person or thing. In this metaphor, Frank mourns the fact that his love was never returned by comparing it to the way that religious people one-sidedly worship their God.

Frank could also referring to religions where homosexuality is considered a sin. Throughout the song, Frank is “in love” with a boy, but he may also be inferring that his relationship with God is one of unrequited favour due to his ‘sinful’ homosexuality.

line: Taxi driver
vault_lines: I guess it couldn't hurt me
meaning:
Like balancing steak knives on your head is very dangerous and challenging, Frank is also having a hard time balancing all of these lives he’s leading—his personal life with those close to him, his private life and his secret (at the time) sexuality, and his public life as a performer. When this song was recorded he still had not written his famous blog post, hence his “disguise” that he mentions in the next line.



He believes that the slightest misstep can kill his career, just like the slightest movement can push over the steak knife and make it cut through his head. Unfortunately, identifying as LGBTQ+ is still seen as a calculated risk that can hurt performers professionally. This is especially true of male performers, who are expected to live up to society’s conceptual ideal of masculinity.

In recent years, the hip hop community has become much more openly supportive of its LGBTQ+ artists, in small part because of Frank’s frankness about his struggles with his sexuality.

line: “Bobo, you need prayer”
vault_lines: "Bobo, you need prayer"
meaning:
Bobo* is a common slang term among the Hispanic diaspora meaning “foolish person” or “dummy.” This further places the taxi driver in the immigrant community, exasperated by this bougie kid’s first world problems.

In a Sierra Leonean language, Krio, “bobo” means “boy.” This reading would both emphasize the immigrant roots of the taxi driver and potentially allude to the fourth track on the album, “Sierra Leone.”

The taxi driver’s insistence that Frank “needs prayer” can be read as a sincere belief that it might be the most helpful thing for Frank at that moment, or it might be exasperation speaking (see also: “that boy needs Jesus”). However, it is the only tonic that Frank’s pseudo-shrink prescribes.

* This can also be heard as “but boy,” and provide a double meaning, but Channel Orange’s liner notes confirm “bo bo” is the correct lyric.

line: It’s rush hour So take the streets if you wanna Just outrun the demons, could you?
vault_lines: So take the streets if you wanna
meaning:
“Rush hour” refers to is the busiest times of day for automobile traffic. In the evenings, this usually takes place around 5-7pm as commuters travel home from work. There is an a slight irony here, as the end of work suggests a release from the hustle and stress of the day, but Frank Ocean’s problems seem to be following him home.



As Frank is in no particular hurry, he tells the taxi driver that he can take the streets where traffic is likely to be most congested, as this gives him more time to talk and get his emotions out. However, this time and space also gives Frank time to reflect on his problems, so he’s asking the driver to find a middle ground between slow enough to let him express his feelings and fast enough that he doesn’t get swallowed up by them.

Going further, Frank’s mention of his “demons” so plainly in the first verse helps to set the song’s overall tone of reflective, pseudo-religious angst. No matter where the taxi or this song goes, he can’t get past his melancholy, “unnatural” thoughts. He knows the situation which is causing his sadness cannot continue the way it has been, and he is just trying to escape this judgement day for a little longer.

This inner turmoil adds up to a secondary state of “rush hour” inside Frank’s head.

line: I can’t tell you the truth about my disguise I can’t trust no one
vault_lines: I can't tell you the truth about my disguise
meaning:
Frank Ocean is struggling with revealing that he is in love with a man, and feels unable to live his life openly and truthfully.

He is forced to live a lie to protect himself and his feelings, but he has gone so deeply into it that perhaps he doesn’t know what the truth is anymore. Or perhaps he is so afraid to reveal the truth that he cannot bring himself to.

line: Leave the meter runnin’
vault_lines: Leave the meter runnin'
meaning:
Frank implies that he needs this taxi ride more for the opportunity to talk to somebody than to get somewhere. Usually, a taxi driver will start and stop the meter at the beginning and end of the journey. What he wants to say is going to take a while, so Frank invites his cabbie to ignore the destination and just leave the meter running while he spills out his emotions.

He would also have to pay a shrink for an hour of therapy, so he’s willing to pay the cabbie for his advice.

line: Taxi driver
vault_lines: I guess it couldn't hurt me
meaning:
Frank asks the cabbie to serve as his “shrink”—a catch-all term for psychiatrists, psychologists, and psychotherapists—by listening to him talk about his problems and concerns. The line itself mirrors the convention that professional therapists charge an hourly rate. Frank is so desperate, or so strapped, that he asks an untrained stranger this role. After all, someone who knows nothing about the situation might be able to bring Frank some much-needed perspective.



Taxi drivers are frequently seen as therapeutic windows by passengers as a way to vent personal frustration, anger, or other emotions. According to one study, as many as 70% of those surveyed see taxi rides as a time for reflection on one’s life or one’s day. Because of this, taxi drivers sometimes find themselves acting as a confidant for their contemplative customers. The privacy of the taxi gives these conversations an almost confessional aspect—as the taxi driver must keep their eyes on the road, the passenger can almost feel like they are speaking anonymously.

In fact, this trope of taxi driver as therapist has had some significant moments in popular culture—both on film, as in Taxi Driver—and in real life: Stockholm briefly posted psychotherapists in the backs of their cabs, allowing riders to receive professional consultations on the go.

line: I told him, “Don’t curse me”
vault_lines: I told him, "Don't curse me"
meaning:
This song uses religion as a metaphor for unrequited love. So when the Taxi driver says “God is great,” he connects that to the curse of un-returned love. He’s already worshiping his own god (his love) and it’s only caused him pain. The last thing he thinks he needs is another deity to worship.



It’s also true that many religions curse those who are not heterosexual, and Frank is in the process of confessing this about himself.

Because of very sparse education in American schools about world religions including Islam, many connect Muslims exclusively to radical Islam, and the phrase, “Allahu Akbar” exclusively to a jihadist war cry. Perhaps Frank, unaware of the Arabic phrase’s real translation, assumes that what the driver is saying is somehow derogatory or chastises. The following lyric clarifies the driver’s intentions.

line: He said, “Allahu akbar”
vault_lines: He said, "Allahu akbar"
meaning:
The taxi driver speaks Arabic, and the phrase “Allahu Akbar,” meaning “God is [the] greatest,” is a common protective oath used in Islam—including at the beginning of the adhan, the Islamic call for prayer.

The taxi driver gives Frank advice, essentially saying, “No matter how big your problem is, God is the greatest, and He is capable of anything.” Most religions believe that humbling yourself before the creator’s power will bring perspective and wisdom to face life’s challenges. Perhaps he genuinely feels for Frank and doesn’t know any other way to help him.

He could also be repeating the common saying as an exasperated “curse” against the sad sack in his back seat (like a Catholic might sarcastically say “saints preserve us”).

Frank running into a Muslim cab driver is no coincidence. In 2017, the New York Taxi Workers Alliance estimated that between 60 and 70 percent of its members were Muslim.

meaning:
Tyler became infamous in his early days for his immensely rowdy live shows.

He was arrested after a 2014 headlining performance at South by Southwest. Tyler reportedly ordered fans to shove through security gates, inciting chants of “PUSH, PUSH, PUSH”. When hundreds rushed in, filling the venue past max capacity, Tyler’s microphone was turned off, at which point the scene reportedly almost became violent.

Five years later, a surprise show in Britain, Tyler’s first after being banned from the country in 2015, had to be shut down by police due to similar safety concerns.

As wild and energetic as his shows are, Tyler’s still bummed out, because the one person he wants to be there is absent.

Goldfish are common pets, but the use of “gold-” accentuates the genuine connection Tyler strives for, but has never achieved.

line: I know you sick of me talkin’ ’bout cars (Skrrt) But what the fuck else do you want from me? That is the only thing keepin’ me company Purchase some things until I’m annoyed These items is fillin’ the void (Void) Been fillin’ it for so long I don’t even know if it’s shit I enjoy (Ohh! Woo!)
vault_lines: But that don't mean nothin', nothin'
meaning:
Tyler has mentioned cars quite a few times in this song alone, not to mention in his previous albums. On his 2013 project Wolf, he literally has a song titled “Bimmer” where he compares the physical qualities of a woman to a BMW. Two years later on Cherry Bomb, he would have a song titled “2SEATER,” in which he describes speeding away on a romantic escapade.

This album itself is laced with vehicle inspired lines, from its radio skits to Tyler “switching gears and swerving” on his opponents. As a matter of fact, the first two lines spoken on the album in “Foreword” are:

How many cars can I buy ‘til I run out of drive?
How much drive can I have 'til I run out of road?

By now, listeners may be annoyed with hearing Tyler talk about vehicles, but he admits that they’re the only thing that can keep him occupied in his lonely life. He buys them and other random luxuries, hoping that these material pleasures can mitigate the loneliness he feels inside.

As a result of this materialism, Tyler doesn’t even know if buying these things makes him happy anymore or if he just does it for the sake of doing it.

The phrase is most famously known for being used in Snow White when the Queen asks; “Magic Mirror on the wall, who’s the fairest of them all?”

In Shrek, Lord Farquaad uses The Magic Mirror to ask; “Mirror, mirror on the wall, is this not the most perfect kingdom of them all?”.  It’s also been used in many other fairy tales, with the line slightly changing and varying in different movies and books.

Tyler is using the mirror to ask a rhetorical question about who the loneliest of them all is, which, obviously, is him.

meaning:

A night line is the name often given to services that provide anonymous overnight listening and emotional support for mainly young people. You could say Tyler could use some of this given his lamenting about his ex throughout the song.

A lot of office workplaces will have you dial 9 before a phone number in order to get an outside line to differentiate between internal and external numbers. Frank is essentially saying whether it’s the middle of the night or you’re stuck at work find the time to make the call to the ones you care about, because you may not get the chance again.

meaning:
“Bitch” is a pejorative slang term for a woman, but it originally meant “female dog.” Tyler uses the word to link his inability to foster a connection with another living thing when he was younger to his relationship troubles today. Tyler is actually allergic to dogs, which he tweeted about in 2014:

https://twitter.com/tylerthecreator/status/481830441570533378

“Threw a ball” could mean that he literally didn’t throw a ball, as in girls didn’t like him because he didn’t play sports growing up. It could be an analogy for the small talk and effort that’s usually required to strike up a romantic relationship, since this song is mostly about how the people around Tyler don’t go out of their way to reach out to him.

“Stem” also continues the garden theme throughout the album.

line: Ask me how I’m really doin’ So I never have to press that 911
vault_lines: (Call me) How you doin'?
meaning:
Tyler could simply mean here that he never wants to be in a situation in which he might harm himself or attempt to commit suicide, and then have to call 911 in an emergency.

Additionally, the way Tyler pauses after saying “9” could be a reference a nine millimeter gun; he wants someone to really care and ask him how he’s doing so he won’t want to kill himself by “pressing” the gun against his head.

This line rounds off the track by going deepest into the consequences of exclusion and loneliness – Tyler is telling us what can happen when people have nobody to ask how they’re doing, just to talk to them once. Maybe we can be the ones to ask.

line: I’m the loneliest man alive But I keep on dancing to throw ’em off I’m gon’ run out of moves ’cause I can’t groove to the blues If you know any DJs, tell ’em to call me at 911...
vault_lines: (Call me, call me, call me) Uh
meaning:
In “Lone”, Tyler raps:

Ya boy seem happy as fuck but truthfully ya boy lonely

Tyler’s public persona is very funny and outgoing. From having a footrace with Kanye West to making waffles on a cooking show, he presents a carefree image. Here he’s saying it’s a facade—the dancing and the acting is just to mask his loneliness.

Tyler then goes on to say that he is going to “run out of moves” because he can’t “dance to the blues”, most likely using the analogy to explain that he can’t fully express himself (keep dancing) because he is not emotionally capable enough to express pain or sorrow properly. This is a very real tendency that leads to depression in many cases; seemingly counterintuitive, but not being able to express sorrow is oftentimes a killer cause for depression than just being ‘happy’.
